title: Which pile has more particles?
hook: Water weighs more than carbon here. Does heavier mean more particles?

knows: that matter is made of atoms and molecules
that different atoms have different masses
doesNotKnow: that a mole is a fixed count of particles (about 6.02 x 10^23)
that molar mass is the mass of one mole

misconception: A mole is a mass, or the heavier pile must hold more particles.
objective: The learner can explain that a mole is a count, so 12 g of carbon and 18 g of water each hold about one mole (about 6.02 x 10^23 particles); the water weighs more because each molecule is heavier.

claims.source: BIPM, The International System of Units (SI Brochure), 9th ed. 2019: Avogadro constant N_A = 6.02214076 x 10^23 mol^-1, exact.

claims.text: Molar masses: carbon about 12.011 g/mol, water about 18.015 g/mol, aluminium 26.982 g/mol, iron 55.845 g/mol (so one mole of iron is about 56 g).
claims.source: IUPAC/CIAAW standard atomic weights (conventional values C 12.011, H 1.008, O 15.999, Al 26.982, Fe 55.845); water = 2 x 1.008 + 15.999 = 18.015 g/mol.

claims.text: 12 g of carbon and 18 g of water are each about 1 mole, about 6.02 × 10²³ particles.
claims.source: 12/12.011 = 0.9991 mol; 18/18.015 = 0.9992 mol; times N_A = 6.017 x 10^23 particles each (node script).

claims.text: A water molecule is about 18 atomic mass units and a carbon atom about 12, so each water molecule is heavier (18 against 12, in the same units).
claims.source: Molar mass in g/mol equals the particle's mass in daltons (atomic mass units), by the definition of the mole and dalton (SI Brochure 2019, IUPAC Gold Book 'dalton'): 18.015 Da vs 12.011 Da. | v2 (2026-10-14): text/stage revised after learner review; previous verification void, needs re-check. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: CIAAW conventional atomic weights: H2O 2(1.008) + 15.999 = 18.015, C 12.011; molar mass in g/mol equals particle mass in Da (SI Brochure 9th ed. 2019, not re-opened). Reveal text '18 against 12, in the same units' matches.

claims.text: On the stage each dot stands for 1/40 of a mole (about 1.5 × 10²² particles); the outlined box of two rows of 40 dots is one mole, labelled "full box" until the reveal names it.
claims.source: Representation choice: dots = round(moles x 40); 6.022e23 / 40 = 1.51e22. | v2 (2026-10-14): text/stage revised after learner review; previous verification void, needs re-check. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: DISPUTED. Demo.tsx draws COLS = 20 dots per row, so the outlined box is two rows of 20 dots (40 dots); the claim's 'two rows of 40 dots' reads as 80 dots. Other parts check: PER_MOL = 40, 6.02214076e23 / 40 = 1.506e22, stage label 'full box', reveal names the crowd one mole. Fix (builder): 'the outlined box of two rows of 20 dots (40 in all) is one mole'.

claims.text: Because a mole has a fixed count, chemists count particles by weighing.
claims.source: Standard practice; e.g. Atkins, Jones & Laverman, Chemical Principles, 'The mole' (amount of substance from mass via molar mass).

recall.question: One mole of iron weighs about 56 g; one mole of aluminium about 27 g. Which holds more atoms: 56 g of iron or 27 g of aluminium?
recall.why: Each is one mole, and a mole is a fixed count, about 6.02 x 10^23 atoms, whatever the atoms weigh.
